newsitem.title: MEXICO: FOCUS - Mexico primary Cetes rates set to rebound.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Mexico primary Cetes rates set to rebound.

text.p: Mexican primary Cetes rates are set to rebound, after having tumbled sharply since the start of the year, analysts said on Thursday.
Sharply higher secondary rates, and a rapidly weakening peso all point to a rebound in rates at Banco de Mexico's auction next week.
"What we have seen in the markets confirms my view that this should be the floor," brokerage house Interacciones economist Alonso Cervera said.
Rates on the bellwether 28-day paper have fallen for ten straight weeks, dropping to 18.59 percent last Tuesday.
"The downward trend has been cut off," brokerage house Abaco economist Martin Creixell said.

Cetes rates have touched lows not seen since the peso devaluation of December 1994. Rates just before the peso crash hovered around 20.07 percent. Following the peso collapse, the return on one-month paper soared, peaking at 74.84 percent in April 1995.
Today's trade also reflected the peso's influence. As the benchmark 48-hour peso buckled by 17.6 centavos, overnight Cetes rates rocketed 375 basis points higher to 22 percent.
Rates had recently fallen on strong inflows of capital into Mexican markets that were keeping the peso strong, and on expectations of lower inflation.
But the risk of peso weakness has put a damper on the enthusiasm for the Treasury bill paper recently, knocking down demand sharply.
"We have seen a significant drop in demand for Cetes in the past two weeks," Cervera said.
As recently as January 28 demand was a strong 14.38 billion pesos.
Last week, however, demand fell to 7.72 billion pesos, down from 8.95 billion pesos the week down. In the past two weeks, demand has fallen 44 percent, Cervera said.
"It reflects that investors are starting to become cautious about a possible rebound in the exchange rate and in interest rates," Cervera added.
Investors are also showing some concern that key mid-term elections set for July this year could add to market turmoil, adding more pressure on Treasury bill rates, analysts added.
"People are seeing there may be some volatility before the elections," Abaco's Creixell said.
